---
title: "Tools"
subtitle: "The five MCP tools Whetstone exposes, plus the out-of-band maintenance & sharing CLI."
---

Whetstone is a stdio MCP server. A skill (or your agent) calls these tools around each task — you
rarely call them by hand. All state is a git-tracked, per-skill store, organized into **learnings**
(soft preferences) and **issues** (mandatory rules) grouped by **scope** (a short label for what a
preference is about, e.g. `currency-formatting`) — see **[Concepts](concepts.qmd)** for the full
vocabulary this page assumes.

## `attach` {#attach}

```python
attach(skill: str, path: str | None = None) -> dict
```

Register a skill so Whetstone tracks its learned layer. Scaffolds a git-tracked store for `skill`,
organized by **[scope](concepts.qmd#scopes)**, and records it in the registry. **Idempotent** —
attaching an already-attached skill is a no-op that reports `already_attached`. `recall` / `capture`
create a store lazily if you skip this, so `attach` is optional setup. `path` is an optional
reference to the target skill's location, recorded as provenance.

Returns a summary: `skill`, `slug`, `path` (store dir), and `created`.

## `recall` {#recall}

```python
recall(skill: str, intent: str, learnings_k: int | None = None) -> dict
```

Call at the **start** of any task that might use an attached skill — call it blindly; an empty
result is fine. Pass `intent` as a concrete, **elaborated** description of what you're about to
produce, expanding vague requests into their specific dimensions (e.g. *"styling a table: color
palette, number formatting, column alignment, row banding, density"*) — not the user's raw words.
Retrieval quality lives and dies on this: *"make a table styled well"* embeds nowhere near a scope
named *"currency formatting"*.

Returns the weighted **learnings** (soft preferences) and **issues** (mandatory constraints) that
match the intent, ready for the skill to apply. `learnings_k` optionally caps how many learnings
come back. Each entry is tagged with its `origin` — `"skill"` (this skill's own store) or
`"global"` (a preference promoted to the cross-skill **[learned global layer](concepts.qmd#global-layer)**);
prefer the more specific `"skill"` entry when the two disagree.

The payload also carries `conflicts` — an always-present list (`[]` when clean) flagging pairs,
within the entries just returned, where a learning affirms what a co-returned issue forbids. It's a
read-only annotation over the finalized set (never a retrieval decision): the issue always wins.
Each item tags an `origin` alongside each id (`a_origin`/`b_origin`), since the skill store and the
global store mint ids independently and can collide, plus an `a_skill`/`b_skill` — the literal
`skill` to pass to `revise` for that side, since a `"global"`-origin entry must be revised through
the reserved global slug, not the current skill.

## `capture` {#capture}

```python
capture(skill, polarity, body, scope, provenance=None, run_id=None, confirm=False) -> dict
```

Call the moment you act on user feedback about output from an attached skill, when it's something
**new**. Cues: a fix (*"right-align that"*), a preference (*"I like muted palettes"*), a rejection
(*"no, not like that"*), or approval of a specific choice.

Classify it: taste / preference → `polarity:"learning"`; a mistake to never repeat or an explicit
"always/never" rule → `polarity:"issue"` (word the body objectively). Generalize the feedback into a
scoped rule of a few short sentences that capture the user's *why*. `capture` dedupes and
conflict-checks against existing entries before writing.

**`possible_contradiction`** (§M7c, experimental — gated by `same_polarity_contradiction_check`,
**off by default**, opt-in): a near-duplicate **learning** whose wording actually flips against the existing one —
a small, hand-picked antonym/negation lexicon catches the clearest cases ("left" vs. "right", a
negation word on only one side) — returns this status (the existing entry's id and its current
wording as `existing_body`, the new `candidate_body`, and a short `note`) instead of silently
reinforcing. Nothing is written. This check is deterministic, so re-calling `capture` with the same
body flags again rather than resolving anything — resolve it via `revise` on the flagged `entry_id`
instead: `action:"reinforce"` with no `body` if it genuinely was a duplicate (bumps recurrence
without re-running this check). If it truly was a contradiction, don't `"reinforce"` with a
reworded `body` — that keeps the old recurrence and could push a single opposite observation
straight to promotion; `"remove"` the entry instead (not `"weaken"`, which only lowers recurrence
and typically leaves it indexed, so a fresh `capture` would flag again) and THEN `capture` the
corrected preference fresh, at its own honest recurrence. **Confirm with the user before calling
`"remove"`** — this is a heuristic signal, not a user decision, and removing a learning is
dial-governed (it deletes immediately outside supervised mode, unlike an issue contradiction, which
always confirms). This narrows, but does not remove, the general limitation that embeddings alone
can't separate a same-polarity contradiction from a paraphrase — see [Concepts](concepts.qmd) and
`LEARNING_SKILLS_DESIGN.md` §7.

On a committed change `capture` (and `revise`) return a short human-facing **`confirmation`** string
— *"Captured: currency columns — …. Re-applies on future great-tables runs."* — so the agent can
tell you what it recorded and that it will stick. The learned layer is otherwise invisible; the
tool descriptions instruct the model to relay it.

## `revise` {#revise}

```python
revise(skill, entry_id, action, body=None, scope=None, run_id=None, confirm=False) -> dict
```

Call when feedback concerns a learning or issue that `recall` **already showed** you (use its `id`).
`action` is one of:

| action | when |
| --- | --- |
| `reinforce` | the user repeated a preference (raises its weight) |
| `weaken` | the user contradicted one (lowers its weight) |
| `promote` | a preference should become an always/never rule (reword required) |
| `demote` | a hard rule should soften back to a preference |
| `remove` | the user rejected it outright |

Confirmation-gated: destructive actions require `confirm=True`. Optional `body` / `scope` supply
reworded prose (required for `promote`).

## `metrics` {#metrics}

```python
metrics(skill: str | None = None) -> dict
```

**Reporting only** — never call during normal work. Computes per-skill KPIs from each store's
`events.jsonl` and current state: runs, average learnings-applied-per-run, capture counts by status,
the reinforcement rate (a repeat-correction proxy — the "money metric"), and % survived. KPIs that
need a labeled/calibration set — capture-rate, regressions-prevented, retrieval-precision — are
returned as `{"value": null, "note": …}` rather than guessed. See the **[Metrics](metrics.qmd)** page
for the live numbers and **[Methodology](methodology.qmd)** for how they're produced.

## The out-of-band CLI (not tools)

Some operations are deliberate, human- or schedule-initiated maintenance — they rewrite the whole
store, commit, and can change what the *next* `recall` returns, so they are **command-line
subcommands, never MCP tools** an agent might fire mid-task. They are all safe to run at a session
boundary.

```sh
whetstone compact <skill>          # tidy one store + report advisory behavioral findings
whetstone compact --all            # tidy every store, then *report* cross-skill candidates
whetstone promote <skill> <id>     # lift one learning/issue into the learned global layer
whetstone promote <skill> <id> --cluster  # enact one reported cross-skill candidate, by hand
whetstone export <skill>           # write a shareable preference pack (.tar.gz)
whetstone import <skill> <pack>    # import a pack (dedup-aware: --merge default | --replace)
whetstone doctor <skill>           # read-only health check for the learned loop
```

### `compact` — tidy, and mine for health

`compact` runs two passes. The **structural** pass is auto-applied and always has been: it dedupes
near-duplicate entries, merges overlapping scopes, and retires learnings whose weight has decayed
below threshold (issues are never auto-retired). On top of that, a **behavioral mining** pass reads
the store's `events.jsonl` and reports — **advisory only, never auto-applied** — four health signals:

| finding | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `harden` | a learning you keep reinforcing and never contradict → consider promoting it to an issue |
| `bad_capture` | a scope with repeated captures *and* corrections → the original capture was likely too broad |
| `stale` | a learning `recall` keeps surfacing but you never reinforce, or never surfaces at all → a retire nudge |
| `conflict_residue` | a flagged conflict you never resolved |

Findings are printed and written to a git-ignored `compact-report.md`; enacting one is a manual
`revise`. Only the safe structural pass ever mutates automatically — the same conservatism `compact`
has always had. See **[Concepts → Maintenance](concepts.qmd#maintenance)**.

### `compact --all` — report cross-skill promotion candidates

With `--all`, `compact` runs over every attached skill and then looks for a preference you have
taught in several skills. When the same learning recurs across enough distinct skills, it comes back
as a fifth, advisory `global_candidate` finding — never auto-applied. Promotion always asks a human,
regardless of supervision mode, and `--all` is no exception: it **never writes to the global store
itself**. The finding names a representative entry and the exact command to enact it:
`whetstone promote <skill> <id> --cluster`.

### `promote` — lift a preference by hand

`whetstone promote <skill> <id>` moves a single learning or issue into the
**[learned global layer](concepts.qmd#global-layer)** deliberately, re-minting its id there. Use it
when you already know a preference is cross-cutting and don't want to wait for `--all` to notice.
Add `--cluster` to instead enact a whole cross-skill cluster reported by `compact --all` as a
`global_candidate` finding — `<skill> <id>` then name that cluster's representative entry, and the
command writes the representative into the global store and retires every per-skill copy in the
cluster, across all its skills.

### `export` / `import` — preference packs

Sharing your taste is a deliberate human act (never something an agent should do on its own), so it
lives on the CLI. `export` writes a **preference pack** — a `.tar.gz` of your `learnings/` + `issues/`
markdown plus a `pack.toml` manifest (telemetry, the derived index, and git history are excluded).
`import` folds a pack into a store: `--merge` (default) reuses the same dedup + conflict checks
`capture` does — near-duplicates fold in, opposite-polarity clashes are surfaced rather than silently
applied — while `--replace` swaps the store's contents wholesale. Either way **ids are re-minted**, so
a teammate's pack can never collide with yours. See **[Concepts → Preference packs](concepts.qmd#packs)**.

### `doctor` — is the loop actually wired?

The one failure mode Whetstone can hit quietly is a **silent no-op**: a store is attached but the
host never calls `recall`/`capture`, so nothing is learned and nothing looks wrong. `whetstone doctor
<skill>` is a **read-only** diagnostic — it reports whether the store exists, whether recall/capture
events are landing (counts + last timestamp), the backend in use, and the entry counts. If the loop
looks dead (attached but zero recalls) it prints a host-agnostic snippet of operating instructions to
paste into your host. It never edits anything.
